latin: Cum Platonem audimus Palladem et amorem philosophos deos uocantem, ita intelligamus, ut amor sit philosophus ratione uiae, Pallas ratione termini.
translation: When we hear Plato calling Pallas and Love 'philosopher gods,' let us understand it thus: that Love is a philosopher by reason of the way, Pallas by reason of the end.
translation_note: 'ratione uiae' / 'ratione termini' ('by reason of the way' / 'by reason of the end/terminus') is a scholastic distinction between a process and its goal; the thesis is discussed by Farmer as part of the series he begins at thesis 2.12 (farmer1998:22425).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch15, from Latin at farmer1998:22358
attribution: Pico's own opinion, in the doctrine of Plato (section 5>, farmer1998:22132).
doctrine: The thesis glosses Plato's naming of Pallas and Love as 'philosopher gods': Love is a philosopher by reason of the way, the process toward wisdom, Pallas by reason of the end or goal (farmer1998:22358). Farmer's note places the thesis in the same series he begins discussing at thesis 2.12 and states that Pallas recurs elsewhere in Pico as a symbol, though the note is truncated in the material consulted before it names of what (farmer1998:22425).
historiography: Busi and Ebgi print the Latin and an Italian translation of the thesis (busi2014:17341, busi2014:24858), and separately note that Pico's linking of Pallas with philosophy recurs elsewhere in his work, in a discussion of Proverbs 27:11 and a saying they attribute to the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Ta'anit 7a (busi2014:17528).
not_established: Which other work of Pico contains the Proverbs 27:11 / Talmudic parallel that Busi and Ebgi cite is not identified in the material consulted.
The symbolic value Farmer says Pallas 'regularly' carries for Pico is not established by the sources consulted, since his note is cut off before stating it.
